description_full: Weyco Group, Inc. designs, markets, and distributes footwear for men, women, and children in the United States, Canada, Australia, Asia, and South Africa. The company operates in two segments, North American Wholesale and North American Retail. The company offers mid-priced leather dress shoes and casual footwear composed of man-made materials and leather; and outdoor boots, shoes, and sandals under the Florsheim, Nunn Bush, Stacy Adams, and BOGS brands. It engages in the wholesale of its products to footwear, department, and specialty stores, as well as e-commerce retailers in the United States and Canada. The company also operates e-commerce business; and brick and mortar retail stores in the United States. In addition, it has licensing agreements with third parties, who sell its branded apparel, accessories, and specialty footwear in the United States, as well as footwear in Mexico and certain markets overseas. The company was formerly known as Weyenberg Shoe Manufacturing Company and changed its name to Weyco Group, Inc. in April 1990. Weyco Group, Inc. was incorporated in 1906 and is based in Glendale, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: Weyco Group, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $569M market cap on $276M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and -1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 9% cost of capital, a 6-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 40%.

The business throws off $36M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.61× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 33% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $87.1M.

growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.7% over 3 years, 0.6% over 5 years and -1.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 45.8% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (0.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 33.4%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 29%.

people: With about 408 employees, each generates about $677K of revenue, 1.8x the Consumer Cyclical median.

CEO pay is $827K (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (10/10, lower is better).
